assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices and dynamic industry models turned industrial organisation into a quantitative empirical field. The methods are used routinely in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and in applied work well beyond IO.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand framework is clearly credited to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also carries the dynamic-games line (Ericson-Pakes) and the estimation of dynamic oligopoly. Bresnahan, Reiss and Levin made real contributions to empirical IO, but the three-name limit forces a narrow credit that is arguable.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from 1987 to 1995 and has decades of confirmation and wide adoption. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would credit Bresnahan in place of Levinsohn.
Whether the prize is framed as IO or as econometric method, and the attribution consequences of that framing.
The three-name cap leaves out other significant contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reshaped trade theory and empirics. Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI explain who trades, gains from trade and within-industry reallocation. The framework is a standard workhorse in trade and has also been taken up in macroeconomics and IO.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the central originator of the heterogeneous-firm model. Helpman has a broad and long record in trade theory, including the heterogeneous-firm extensions. Redding contributed substantially, mostly in quantitative and spatial extensions, and is less clearly part of the core discovery.
assessment.maturity: The core work is from the 2000s and has been confirmed by a large body of firm-level evidence. It is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with Helpman's separate candidacy on the political economy of trade policy (B049).
Whether Krugman's earlier prize is judged to have absorbed part of the novelty of new trade theory.
Melitz-Redding's own contributions on welfare gains may blur the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Autor's task-based approach to technology and the China-shock evidence on local labour markets changed how economists and policymakers think about trade, automation and wage inequality. The work is highly influential in both research and public debate.
assessment.attribution: The task framework and polarisation evidence are strongly linked to Autor. Hanson is central to the trade-shock literature with Autor and Dorn. Katz has a long record on skill-biased technical change and wage structure. Dorn is also a central co-author of the China-shock papers, so the three-name cap truncates credit.
assessment.maturity: The work spans from the 1990s to the 2010s. The China-shock results have been debated and refined, but the core findings have largely held up.
uncertainties: Task-framework credit also belongs to co-authors such as Levy and Murnane, who are not on the list.
Dorn's exclusion, and the split of credit between the technology and trade strands.
Continuing debate about magnitudes and the persistence of the trade-shock effects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The intertemporal approach to the current account, the New Open Economy Macroeconomics ('redux' model) and the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles provided the micro-founded foundation of modern international macroeconomics. The textbook and policy influence is large.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff are the two clearly identified authors of the framework and the puzzles, which makes the pairing clean. Other researchers, such as Lane, Gopinath and Devereux, extended the framework but are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: The core work is from the 1990s and has had decades of use. Some empirical predictions have a mixed record.
uncertainties: Rogoff also appears in a separate candidacy on financial crises (B022), so the prize rationale needs to be defined.
Weaker empirical validation of some exchange-rate predictions.
The relative weight of the theory versus the policy-puzzle contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Correspondence and audit studies gave credible causal evidence of labour-market discrimination and made the measurement of discrimination a standard empirical method. The 2004 resume experiment is among the most-cited papers in labour economics, and the approach has been widely replicated across settings.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are the identifiable authors of the landmark study. Charles is credited for related work on discrimination and prejudice. The audit-study method has earlier origins (for example, Heckman and Siegelman), which are outside the listed names, so credit for the method is only partial.
assessment.maturity: The central work dates from 2004, with replication and extension over two decades. The finding is well confirmed.
uncertainties: Novelty of the method relative to earlier audit studies.
Mullainathan's other work in behavioural economics could either strengthen or blur the prize rationale.
Interpretation limits of audit designs (for example, the Heckman critique).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Hsieh-Klenow framework quantifies how misallocation of inputs across firms accounts for cross-country TFP gaps. It gives a measurable, widely applied explanation for income differences and links micro data to growth and development.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) are the joint originators of the measurement framework. Restuccia and Rogerson (the latter not on this list) developed the parallel and contemporaneous misallocation theory, so credit is shared and arguably incomplete.
assessment.maturity: The core work is from 2008 to 2009. It has substantial follow-on work, but the interpretation of measured misallocation (adjustment costs, markups and measurement error) is still contested.
uncertainties: Rogerson's absence from the list, and Restuccia's parallel claim.
Sensitivity of the results to data and measurement error.
Comparison with the 2025 growth prize and other recent growth awards.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rubinstein's alternating-offers model (1982) gave non-cooperative bargaining a tractable foundation and linked it to Nash's solution. Rubinstein-Wolinsky then carried it into decentralised markets. The ideas underpin search-and-bargaining models used in labour, monetary and market-design theory.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is the clear originator of the alternating-offers result. Wolinsky is central to the market-bargaining extension. Binmore's role in the strategic bargaining literature is real but secondary to these two.
assessment.maturity: The work is more than four decades old and fully absorbed into the canon, so timing is not an issue. Its long maturity also means the contribution has been integrated widely, so assessing its marginal prize-level impact is harder.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the contribution as already recognised through related game-theory and mechanism prizes.
Rubinstein's critical stance toward applied economics may affect how the case is framed.
Stahl's parallel contribution to the finite-horizon model is not credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: 'Credit Cycles' (1997) showed how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks, and it is a pillar of modern macro-finance and of post-crisis models of financial frictions. The framework is widely used in policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the two clear originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist worked on the financial accelerator, a related but distinct strand. Bernanke-Gertler's earlier accelerator work is partly recognised through Bernanke's 2022 prize.
assessment.maturity: The core work is from the 1990s, with strong post-2008 relevance and extensive follow-up. Some of its empirical performance is mixed.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize for banking and financial crises, which may reduce the marginal case.
Whether the prize should instead include Gertler for the financial accelerator.
Empirical support for the collateral-constraint channel is less clear than the theory.
